doc.title: Bill Easley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 1, 2021

title: First New York years, Juilliard and quitting the bank job
summary: Studying with Joe Allard, running out of money, bank job, then quitting for a road gig with a rock band.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So you learned to read and you became versatile, and when you got to New York you started hanging out, I mean did you — what was your first steady gig in music when you got to New York?

Okay, good question. In other words I worked and saved my money before I went to New York, you know, that summer. And even my sisters gave me a hundred dollars apiece. So I had it all figured — I knew how much money — and I went to Juilliard part time and I had my money set aside for how much my tuition was going to be. I was just going part time, plus I was studying with Joseph Allard. I’m not sure if you know who Joseph Allard was, and that was a great, great, great person to run across at 18 years old you know. And, but my money ran out pretty quickly you know, because, and you’ve got a room and it’s $12 a week or whatever, and you know food. And that money, I thought that money would last for a year but after a few months man I got one of the few day jobs that I ever had in my life and it was working at what was then First National City Bank. And I was making $60 a week on my day job you see. And that was my — but I got into, I started working as a musician pretty soon so I quit that job after a few months because somebody — I was doing occasional jobs anyway, playing here and there. And then I went out on the road with a rock — and they called me at work on Monday. “Man my tenor player didn’t call up man, I need you to come and go to Hazelton, Pennsylvania with us. You know? And I’ll pay you $125 a week. And I’m making $60 at the bank. And the guy that called me for the gig, he told me at that time that he would pay me $75 on weeks that we didn’t work. Naturally that was a big lie, you understand? But I said, so I went to my foreman, oh Walter was his name. I worked in “Incoming Mail” you understand? And my number was 132. And I’d open the mail and I’d put it in the pigeon hole and so on. But I’m hanging out all night ‘til 4 o’clock in the morning in these joints sitting in and playing. So I’d get to work man, and if you made a mistake they would call out your number. You know? So all day long you would hear “132” and you’d have to go back and correct the mistake. But it’s so funny, so this guy calls me for a gig in Hazelton, Pennsylvania, on a Monday. And I don’t even know how he got in touch with me at work

but he called me. And he said, “Man you’ve got to — we’ll pick you up at your apartment house” and so on. So I had to go to my foreman and tell him, “Look man, I just got my big break in show business and I know I should give you two weeks notice.” But he said, “No I can’t start a prison.” So I quit my job and I go out and they are waiting for me uptown. And it was a four piece band and there were three girl dancer/singers. And so I hadn’t even met them before. And it’s like a station wagon with a trailer pulling the instruments and so on, and there’s eight, nine people in there. And I’m like young. I’m like Gomer Pyle. I was Gomer Pyle most of my life. When I think back how Gomer I was back in those days. And so I’m meeting them, “Oh this is our new saxophone player.” Before we could get over the George Washington Bridge, and I said, “Oh yeah and I quit my job.” And the girls said, “You quit your what?” And I knew that there was probably trouble ahead, and there was, there was. I haven’t had a day job since.
A steady gig may be the most accurate oxymoron there is.
There you go. I’ve never heard of one, unless you work “Cats” for like fifteen years or something like that.
Yeah, we’re going to get to that.
